Flying 250 miles above the Earth, the International Space Station (ISS) 
provides a platform for research to improve life on Earth, enable space 
exploration, and understand the universe. This Researcher’s Guide is 
intended to help potential ISS combustion science researchers plan 
experiments utilizing the microgravity environment in order to understand 
how heat and mass transport phenomena coupled with chemistry affect 
combustion behavior and fire safety. It covers the nature of the acceleration 
environment on ISS, available facilities for conducting combustion research, 
examples of previous microgravity investigations, and current combustion 
science and fire safety projects being developed for execution on the ISS.

1. Microgravity, or weightlessness, alters many observable phenomena 
within the physical and life sciences. Systems and processes affected by 
microgravity include surface wetting and interfacial tension, multiphase 
flow and heat transfer, multiphase system dynamics, solidification, and 
fire phenomena and combustion. Microgravity induces a vast array of 
changes in organisms ranging from bacteria to humans, including global 
alterations in gene expression and 3-D aggregation of cells into tissue-like 
architecture.

investigations.title: Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment
moon_base_score_notes: crew-relevant solid materials
investigations.objective: One of the major goals of this investigation was to quantify the sizes that the liquid smoke particulate achieves in low gravity and to relate the droplet size distribution to the smoke generation and smoke transport conditions in the experiment. A numerical code was to be developed to predict the smoke droplet growth as a function of the fuel pyrolysis rate, the thermodynamic properties of the pyrolysis vapor, and the flow environment.
investigations.hypothesis:
The three hypotheses that motivated this investigation:
In a μg environment, with the absence of the strong buoyancy-induced flows, smoke particle growth from a pyrolyzing/smoldering source, as a result of nucleation, condensation, and coagulation, will lead to larger particles compared to those produced in 1g. The formation of the larger particles is favored by the expected higher vapor concentration and smoke residence times near the source due to the reduced velocities and mixing at μg conditions. In particular, it is hypothesized that liquid aerosol smokes produced in microgravity will exhibit substantially larger droplet sizes than under the same conditions in normal gravity (with a corresponding decrease in the particle number density for the same mass of smoke). The change in the size distribution and number density will, in turn, affect the response of the smoke detectors and possibly result in some detectors not producing an alarm when exposed to this smoke.
investigations.approach: The crew installed the near field hardware in the Glovebox, attached the Far Field Box to the Glovebox, and positioned the video cameras. The operator then ran the self diagnostic procedures on the two smoke detectors and activated the video cameras, turned on the igniter for a predefined period of time (15 to 60 seconds), and initiated the thermophoretic soot samplers to sample the smoke. The actual duration of each combustion event was typically 2 minutes. After flight, the particulate collected on the thermophoretic probes were analyzed using a Transmission Electron microscope (TEM) to determine primary and aggregate particle dimensions. The remains of the samples were weighed to determine their mass loss. The digital data was transcribed from the video record and analyzed to determine the response of the detectors. Once the flight mass loss rates were determined, 1-g operation conditions to produce the same loss were determined.The measurements were made using smoke generated by overheated  spacecraft materials where variables such as the sample temperature, flow field, and particle aging time were more rigorously controlled.
investigations.research_impacts: The SAME experiment will provide technology for an advanced fire detector for future spacecraft that will be used for long duration missions. SAME will provide quantitative data on the sensitivity of these detectors to reduced gravity smokes that will allow evaluation of the adequacy of these existing technologies using relevant data. The current Fire Prevention, Detection, and Suppression (FPDS) program plan allows for the re-evaluation of future sensor technology, to allow new technology and capability to be utilized. The results from SAME are needed to provide the reduced gravity baseline data against which future detection technology developments can be evaluated.The smoke detectors developed from the results of SAME can also be useful in other extreme environments on Earth, such as submarines or underwater laboratories. Accurate detection of smoke in these environments can save lives.

Leaks, fires, and spills are some of the most significant hazards that must be accounted for in the 
design of the environmental control and life-support system on spacecraft. While prevention is 
certainly the first line of defense against a fire, early detection of a overheat event or an actual 
fire allows the crew to respond before the hazard gets out of control. The limited options 
available for response to a spacecraft fire increase the importance of detecting the fire in an 
earlier stage of its development than is typical for terrestrial applications.  This report describes 
the outcomes of the Smoke Aerosol Measurements Experiment (SAME), an experiment 
conducted in the Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) on the International Space Station (ISS) 
to characterize the size distribution of smoke particulate produced in low-gravity from a variety 
of overheated spacecraft materials The absence of gravity can impact not only the formation of 
the smoke particulate but also the aging and coagulation processes that occur as the particulate 
are transported from their source to a detector.

Based on the results of an earlier flight project carried out in the Glovebox of the Space Shuttle, 
(Comparative Soot Diagnostics (CSD)), the soot particles generated and observed in low gravity 
environment tend to be larger in size than those in earth conditions. However, the preliminary 
results of CSD project were not conclusive because of a minor variation of the temperature of hot 
wire which heated the test sample to generate smoke, and also because the CSD apparatus could 
not measure the liquid drops existing in the smoke produced by several of the samples. 
Furthermore, the CSD project was not designed to provide on-orbit measurement of the particle

sections.introduction:
Appropriate design of fire detection systems requires knowledge of both the expected signature of the 
events to be detected and the background levels of the measured parameters.  Terrestrial fire detection 
systems have been developed based on extensive study of terrestrial fires.1, 2 Unfortunately, there is no 
corresponding data set for spacecraft fires and consequently current spacecraft fire detectors were 
developed based upon experience on normal gravity fire behavior and properties. This approach was 
necessary given the absence of data concerning microgravity smoke particulate. However planned 
spacecraft and their planned missions outside of low earth-orbit will require increased reliability of fire 
detection systems in addition to robust false alarm resistance.  Extended lunar-surface missions will 
require systems that are not influenced by lunar dust and other nuisance dust sources.

The absence of buoyant flow increases the residence time in microgravity fires causing substantial 
changes in flame structure. Given the large changes in fire behavior seen in reduced gravity, it is 
reasonable to expect that the signatures and detection requirements of these fires will change. There are 
a number of factors that can be expected to affect the particle size distribution of the smoke from 
spacecraft fires. The absence of buoyant flow in low-gravity increases the residence time in 
microgravity fires and increases the transit time from the reaction zone to the detector.3 The materials 
used in spacecraft are different from those typically used in terrestrial applications where smoke 
properties were previously evaluated. More importantly, the limited options available to respond to a 
spacecraft fire increase the importance of detecting the fire in an earlier stage of its development than is 
typical for terrestrial applications.  All of these effects can be expected to change the smoke particle size 
distribution.  The objective of this work was to make sufficient measurements of smoke from spacecraft 
fires to enable improved design of future detectors.

2. 
Smoke Background 
 
Smoke is a general term that encompasses aerosol materials produced by a number of processes.  In 
particular for non-flaming combustion, the aerosol includes recondensed original material or pyrolysis 
products that can be either liquid or solid.  For flaming combustion, the aerosol includes soot particulate, 
condensed water vapor, and ash particles.  Soot particles dominate the smoke particulate in established 
flaming fires while unburned pyrolysis products and recondensed polymer fragments are produced by 
smoldering and pyrolysis in the early stage of fire growth.  Given the constrained space on any 
spacecraft, the target for the fire detection system is necessarily the early phase and not established 
flaming fires; consequently, the primary target for detection is the pyrolysis products and not the soot.

results suggest that detection methods that can measure 
more than one moment of the size distribution may show

more successful detection and alarm rejection than

SAME-R flight tests were conducted from July 16, to September 9, 2010, successfully completing 66 test points. After SAME-R flight tests, three major post–flight ground tests were performed to improve data reduction process and to validate the lognormal distribution assumption, the key to the moment method employed by SAME and SAME-R.
investigations.research_impacts: Along with the results from the original SAME investigation, the results from SAME-R can lead to technology for an advanced fire detector for future spacecraft that will be used for long duration missions. SAME will provide quantitative data on the sensitivity of these detectors to reduced gravity smokes that will allow evaluation of the adequacy of these existing technologies using relevant data. The current Fire Prevention, Detection, and Suppression (FPDS) program plan allows for the re-evaluation of future sensor technology, to allow new technology and capability to be utilized. The results from SAME are needed to provide the reduced gravity baseline data against which future detection technology developments can be evaluated. The smoke detectors developed from the results of SAME can also be useful in other extreme environments on Earth, such as submarines or underwater laboratories. Accurate detection of smoke in these environments can save lives.

Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment Re-flight (SAMER) is one of the awarded Rapid Turn Around (RTA) 
projects, solicited by NASA Headquarters in June 2009. SAMER is an extension or continuation of Smoke Aerosol 
Measurement Experiment (SAME), which was conducted in the Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) onboard 
the International Space Station (ISS) from September 9 to October 5, 2007. 
 
Generally speaking, SAME experiments were completed successfully in that the apparatus developed for the 
experiments functioned well and desired data from instruments were obtained. However, there was a major problem 
of the SAME experiments. After the thermal precipitators returned to the ground, it was found that all the TEM grids 
were severely contaminated with some unidentified foreign particles, making these grids unusable although some of 
them showed shapes of certain types of smoke particles.  
 
Based on the experience gained from SAME, SAMER included the following modifications: 1) a new test material, 
Pyrell®, an intumescent fire-retardant foam by Foamex, was introduced to replace DBP samples, 2) test conditions 
were broadened including higher heating temperatures and no-flow during sample heating time, and 3) a new 
instrument, M-pass, developed in-house GRC, was used to replace one of the two Commercial Diagnostic 
Enclosures that includes a DustTrak and an ionization detector used in SAME. SAMER flight tests were conducted 
from July 16, to September 9, 2010, successfully completing 66 test points.

and to validate the lognormal distribution assumption, the key to the moment method employed by SAME and 
SAMER. The first ground-based test is the SAMER apparatus flow tests. The objective of the test is to obtain 
accurate dilution ratio data of the P-trak and Dusttrak so that the accuracy of aerosol concentration can be improved.

It was identified that each sample has a significant length of leading section of the resistive wire. This section does not touch the

that contacts the sample material. The control circuitry only controls the total resistance of the heating wire, not individual 
portion of the wire. 
 
Our goal is to find the temperature of the wire that is in contact with the sample material.

Hypothesis:  the temperature difference between the two portions of the wire is caused by different convection heat transfer from 
the two. The wire that is in contact with the sample has less heat loss from the convection heat transfer because about half of its 
surface area is covered by the sample material.

investigations.objective:
The BRE flight program seeks to establish the burning conditions in a quiescent microgravity ambient in terms of material properties.
The specific flight objectives are as follows.
  1. Observe burning behavior in long-duration microgravity for CH4/N2 and C2H4/N2mixtures on porous circular burners of 25  and 50 mm diameter. Consider O2/N2 ambients with various pressures and ambient O2 concentrations and pressures. NASA - considered atmosphere for human space missions will be examined: 14.7 psia, 21 % oxygen: 10.2 psia, 26.5 %; and 8.2 psia, 34 % oxygen. Emphasize fuel conditions that can be related to a diverse range of condensed fuels.
  2. Consider the conditions of Objective 1 for ambients of O2/CO2 (desired).
  3. Consider the conditions of Objectives 1 – 2 for extinction limits.
investigations.hypothesis:
The BRE investigation hypothesizes that there can exist a regime of quasi-steady burning in microgravity as a function of materials properties. Steady burning may never be achieved, and only slowly changing unsteady flames are possible. The proposed tests aboard the ISS aims to query this hypothesis by establishing a range of quasi-steady burning conditions for condensed fuels in the microgravity environment. It is hypothesized that BRE can determine a range of burning conditions in microgravity as a function of heat of gasification, reradiation heat flux, applied radiant heat flux, heat of combustion and smoke point. This could enable the Cone Calorimeter (NASA Test 2) test as a basis for establishing flammability maps for real materials.

The key hypothesis is that the heat of combustion, smoke point, and heat of gasification of the fuel mixture will represent a real solid fuel (or liquid fuel absorbed in an inert matrix). Thus achieved steady burning would represent the potential for real solid fuels to achieve steady burning in microgravity. Other than a candle flame, this has not been shown before.
investigations.approach:
To accomplish the above objectives, flight experiments are proposed. Additionally, preliminary flight tests will be performed to verify the experiment operations and for comparison with ground-based tests.

For each test, conditions will be established for the chamber contents, namely choice of diluent, oxygen concentration, and pressure. Fuel flow will commence followed by ignition. The flames will initially be observed without varying the fuel flow rate. Because burner surface temperature and heat flux will vary, this will allow a broad range of conditions to be observed during a single test. As the surface temperature of the burner increases, and the flame remains steady, a continuous set of data is produced for the flammability map. Eventually either the flame will extinguish, the surface temperature of the burner will equilibrate, or the temperature limit of the heat flux sensor will be reached. At this time the fuel flow will be terminated. So a test should terminate for a given flow rate at extinction, and for continued burning when the burner surface temperature has steadied or the temperature limit of the heat flux sensor is neared.

The extinction limit could be found once the burner temperature has steadied, and the heat flux sensor has not exceeded its limit. At that state, the flow rate can be reduced in small increments, until extinction is observed and the flow rate shut off. Again, in this process, new data is being produced for the flammability map. Ignition limit tests are not proposed for microgravity, but we will explore these under normal gravity. We believe there is better control on Earth-based ignition testing and that these results should carry over to microgravity conditions.

In addition to the flight experiments, in normal gravity testing will continue. These tests will involve gaseous, liquid, and solid fuels. These experiments will further establish the validation of the BRE for 1-g applications and show its usefulness to establish 1-g ignition and extinction limits. As available, drop facility testing will be used to refine procedures, test instrumentation, and help to establish viable flow conditions.

We will also pursue a CFD model for the quiescent microgravity burning. This will also guide us in the flight experiments, and potentially provide a predictive methodology.
investigations.research_impacts: BRE yielded important data relevant to spacecraft fire safety. Quasi-steady burning corresponding to various condensed-phase materials (such as PMMA and Nylon) was observed in microgravity despite the absence of air flow, where the cessation of ventilation is an established step in putting out spacecraft fires. The ongoing combustion without air flow was notably seen in elevated-oxygen atmospheres which are being considered for use in future spacecraft, whereas such flames in a normal atmosphere of 21% oxygen self-extinguished in a short time. While BRE’s results are still preliminary, they suggest that NASA may want to increase use of its alternative flammability Test 2, with the cone calorimeter, where that test can measure material properties corresponding to the microgravity flames observed with the BRE burner.

The Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) experiment is one of six independent experiments that make up the 
Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project for which tests are conducted within 
the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station (ISS).

retired).  The ISS research also benefitted greatly from the work of Parham Dehghani, a doctoral student 
in the Fire Protection Engineering department.

including BRE and the rest of the ACME investigations.  In preparatory drop testing, etc., Dr. Fumiaki 
Takahashi of the Case Western Reserve University (CWRU) served as the Deputy Project Scientist.  For 
ACME’s spaceflight operations, the NASA science team includes Drs. Uday G. Hegde and Vedha Nayagam 
who are also with CWRU. 
 
The ISS operations were conducted in two separate rounds of testing during Increments 58-59 and 63-64.

investigations.objective:
BASS-II results contribute to the combustion computational models used in the design of fire detection and suppression systems in microgravity and on Earth.
Objectives Include:
  1) Study the ignition, flame growth, flame spread, and extinction limits for solid fuels burning in low-velocity forced flows in microgravity.
  2) Begin to bridge the gap between the normal gravity NASA-STD-6001 Test #1 method, ground-based microgravity tests, and actual material flammability in microgravity.
  3) Provide SoFIE PIs with preliminary data to refine Science Requirements.
  4)  Practical, realistic (thicker) fuels in typical geometries will be examined, including slabs, cylinders, and spherical sections.

The primary variables include:
     • Forced flow velocity (speed and direction)
     • Ambient oxygen concentration (via working volume nitrogen vitiation)
     • Sample geometry (rods, spherical section, slabs, films, and fabric sheets
investigations.hypothesis:
BASS–II tests the hypothesis that materials in microgravity, with adequate ventilation, burn as well if not better than the same material in normal gravity with other conditions being identical (pressure, O2
concentration, temperature, etc.). NASA tests and controls materials from a flammability perspective using an upward burning test in normal gravity, which is considered to be the worst-case geometry for
flammability of the material on Earth. However, it may not be conservative for flammability in space. Testing at constant O2 mole fractions permits studying flame spread and extinction at low and high flow speed. We are interested in finding the fundamental limit for a given material.
investigations.approach: To summarize, BASS-II's approach, microgravity combustion tests were performed aboard the International Space Station. Active crew support for real-time “lab partner” operations. The wind tunnel was installed in the Microgravity Science Glovebox which supplied power, imaging, and a level of containment. Fuel samples were mounted inside a small wind tunnel which could impose airflow speeds up to 40 cm/s. Main variables are airflow speed and oxygen concentration (oxygen varied below 21% by adding nitrogen). Flame appearance, flame growth, and spread rates were determined in both the opposed and concurrent flow.
investigations.research_impacts: A primary goal of BASS-II is improved spacecraft fire safety, improved understanding of combustion in space and how to avoid it. If you’re on a mission far from Earth, a fire can be catastrophic. BASS-II helps engineers select the safest materials and improve firefighting methods on future space missions. In outer space, fuels burn as oval balls rather than with an upward pointed cone flame as they do on Earth. This simpler combustion process enables researchers to evaluate computer models of fuel burning. These models can then be used to more accurately study flames on Earth, such as in wildfires, building fires, energy recapture from waste recycling, and other combustion problems.

sections.summary:
The Burning and Suppression of Solids (BASS) experiment hardware is a small flow duct that 
provides containment for small scale burning of solid samples within the Microgravity Science Glovebox 
(MSG) aboard the International Space Station (ISS). A video camera with a data overlay and a 35-mm 
still camera record the combustion events. The controls (ignition, fan speed, etc.) are operated by an 
astronaut while the principal investigator team monitors the experiment from the ground and 
communicates directly with the astronaut. For the first time on ISS, BASS–II utilized MSG working 
volume dilution with gaseous N2. We developed a perfectly stirred reactor model to determine the N2 flow 
time and flow rate to obtain the desired reduced O2 concentration in the working volume for each test. We 
calibrated the model with the Compound Specific Analyzer-Combustion Products (CSA-CP) O2 readings 
offset using the Major Constituents Analyzer reading of the ISS ambient atmosphere data for that day. 
This worked out extremely well for operations, and added a new vital variable, ambient O2 level, to our 
test matrices. The main variables tested in BASS–II were ambient O2 concentration, ventilation flow 
velocity, and fuel type, thickness, and geometry. BASS–II also utilized the onboard CSA-CP for O2 and 
CO readings, and the Carbon Dioxide Monitor for CO2 readings before and after each test. Readings from 
these sensors allow us to evaluate the completeness of the combustion. The O2 and CO2 readings before

sections.results:
Twenty-two test points were obtained with the BASS–II experiments. The wealth of data has been 
catalogued at http://flame.sdsu.edu.

2.1.2.1 Extinction Velocity

Each test is started by establishing a steady flame spread in the presence of a forced flow and then 
reducing the flow velocity in a gradual manner, as shown in Figure 2.1. In the first test, a steady flame 
was established over a 100-μm sample. After the flame propagated across half the sample length at a 
steady spread rate of 2.2 mm/s, the flow was abruptly cut off and the flame was observed to extinguish 
within 2 s, as shown by the radiometer signal drop in Figure 2.2. To pin down the extinction flow 
velocity, a second test was done under the same conditions except the flow velocity was set at 3 cm/s and 
after the flame propagated about half the sample length, the flow was gradually reduced. The flame 
spread rate of the leading edge, as plotted in Figure 2.3, shows that the flame extinguishes at about 30 s 
after ignition. The fan voltage at that time indicates a flow velocity of about 1.1 cm/s. The sequence of 
images in Figure 2.1 shows the pathway to radiative extinction. As the flow speed is gradually reduced 
from about t = 27 s, the flame size starts shrinking and the orange color disappears and the flame becomes 
completely blue, most possibly because of the temperature drop brought about by radiative losses, which 
is enhanced by the increased residence time at low flow velocity. The signal from the radiometer, shown 
in Figure 2.2, is also consistent with a cooling and shrinking flame as the signal starts decreasing from 
right about t = 27 s. After t = 30 s, there is no visible flame and the radiometer data (Figure 2.2) indicate a 
sudden change in slope at that time, possibly because the radiation is emitted mostly by the sample holder 
with the combustion products swept away by the flow.

When tests are repeated with samples of different thicknesses, the extinction velocities are found to 
be about 1 cm/s for 100, 200, and 300 μm and about 1.5 cm/s for 400 μm. At all these thicknesses, the 
fuel can be considered thermally thin because the maximum spread rate was found to be inversely 
proportional to fuel thickness (Ref. 1), a hallmark of a thermally thin regime. However, it must be 
mentioned that there are significant uncertainties in these values as the calibration at such low velocity 
has high error bars. The boundary layer formed by the fuel and the tunnel walls would influence the flow 
velocity seen by the flame. Also, there is a time lag between when the velocity is reduced and when the

sections.abstract:
The effect of opposing flow on flame spread rate over thin solid fuel is investigated with the help of 
scaling theory, a comprehensive computational model, and experiments conducted aboard the 
International Space Station. While spread rate over thin fuels is independent of the opposing flow velocity 
in the thermal regime, in the microgravity regime, where the opposing flow can be very mild or even 
completely absent in the absence of buoyancy-induced flow, the spread rate is known to decrease as the 
opposed flow is reduced. Under certain conditions, this can lead to flame extinguishment at a low enough 
flow velocity. This report combines scaling arguments with computational results to predict a critical flow 
velocity for such flame extinction. Results from the recently conducted limited number of space-based 
tests, presented in this report, seem to confirm the prediction validating the closed-form formula for the 
critical extinction velocity.

investigations.title: Spacecraft Fire Experiment-II
moon_base_score_notes: crew-relevant solid materials
investigations.objective: The objectives of SAFFIRE-II are to determine how rapidly a large scale fire grows in low-gravity and to investigate the low-g flammability limits compared to those obtained in NASA’s normal gravity material flammability screening test.
investigations.hypothesis: This investigation hypothesizes that due to large differences between fire behavior in normal and reduced gravity, the use of terrestrial fires and fire standards to design spacecraft fire safety systems presents an inherent risk to the vehicle because of the significant level of uncertainty. While this approach has been successful thus far, the uncertainty and risk will increase as exploration missions venture further from earth with considerably longer transit times for a safe return. There is a significant lack of microgravity data available for spacecraft designers on which to base their fire safety designs and procedures. To address this knowledge gap, this investigation proposed to conduct large-scale fire safety experiments in an expendable spacecraft without risk to a crew.
investigations.approach: The Saffire-II experiment was performed on the Orbital Science’s Cygnus resupply vehicle after it deberthed from the ISS. As a follow on to the Saffire-I investigation, the Saffire-II investigation added more samples including SIBAL, silicone, structure PMMA, flat PMMA, and PMMA with Nomex. The Saffire-1I flight unit had a sample card installed in the middle of a large flow duct. Air is drawn through the flow duct by fans located at the top of the duct with flow straighteners at the bottom of the experiment module. Saffire-II has a sample card that contains 9 samples, each 5 cm x 29 cm. Depending on the sample material, the Saffire-II was conducted at an air flow velocity of either 20 or 30 cm/s, the flow being either concurrent or opposed.  Once the sample was ignited flame images were captured using two cameras. In addition, thermocouples provided flow, flame, and plume temperatures, two radiometers recorded flame radiation, solid state sensors were used to measure pressure, CO2 and O2 mole faction, and two anemometer tracked flow velocity. All data was compressed, and subsequently downlinked. Details related to samples and experimental parameters are provided in the Experimental Details file in the Science document folder.
investigations.research_impacts: The Saffire-II experiment provides a new way to study a realistic fire on an exploration vehicle, which has not been possible in the past because the risks are too high. Instruments on an unmanned cargo vessel measure oxygen, carbon dioxide, heat, pressure and flame growth, and two video cameras provide views of the flame. Results determine microgravity flammability limits for several spacecraft materials, help to validate NASA’s material selection criteria, and how microgravity and limited oxygen affect flame size. The investigation is crucial for the safety of current and future space missions. Studying fire in small, sealed environments such as the Cygnus cargo supply vehicle benefits fire safety and prevention efforts on Earth, including inside mines, airplanes, or submarines.

investigations.objective:
The two main objectives for BASS are to:
    1.) Begin to bridge the gap between the normal gravity NASA-STD-6001 Test#1 method, ground-based microgravity tests, and actual material flammability in microgravity. The relation between these can be investigated by observing flames burning for the longer times available in flight. Practical, realistic (thicker) fuels in typical geometries will be examined, including wake flames which have characteristics of a fire burning behind another object (for example, a fire burning in tight area which may not be easily accessible).
    2.) Assess the effectiveness of an inert, gaseous extinguishing agent (similar to that used on ISS) in putting out flames over different materials, geometries, preheating, and flow.
investigations.hypothesis: BASS experiments were based on the hypothesis that materials in microgravity, with adequate ventilation, burn as well if not better than the same material in normal gravity with other conditions being identical (pressure, oxygen concentration, temperature, etc.) To test this hypothesis with any but the thinnest materials requires extended microgravity time – longer than available in drop towers or parabolic aircraft.
investigations.approach:
The experiment was conducted aboard the International Space Station (ISS) inside the Microgravity Glove Box (MSG). Custom-made fabric samples consisting of 75% cotton and 25% fiberglass (by mass) measuring were used as a fuel source as well as Nomex fabric and Ultem. A Kanthal wire (29-gage)igniter was used to initiate combustion at one end of the fabric. Airflow was controlled using a variable speed fan, with airflow speeds reaching as high as 40 cm/s. The airflow was directed along the fuel surface in either the opposed or concurrent direction.

This investigation explored two primary air flow configurations; concurrent-flow and opposed-flow. With concurrent-flow air flows in the same direction as the flame spread and in opposed-flow air flows in the opposite direction of flame spread. Flames were observed in the top and edge profiles and data was collected on flame size, shape, color, spread rate, and potential flame quenching. The samples were placed in a small flow duct (76 mm x 76 mm cross section) that allowed for airflow across the fabric. Other sample shapes were utilized as well including spheres and cylinders.
investigations.research_impacts:
Current NASA spacecraft materials selection is based on a standard test method (NASA–STD–6001 Test 1) that segregates material based on 1-g behavior without consideration of low gravity effects. A critical element of this understanding is the radiative heat emission from the flame. These results are used in first order models and predictions of heat release in spacecraft fires and as a means to extend heat release data from tests like the NASA cone calorimeter test (NASA–STD–6001 Test 2) to a performance-based material selection process. Using nitrogen as a flame suppressant in microgravity provides a direct link to current and planned extinguishment techniques.
BASS results provide essential guidance to ground-based microgravity combustion research efforts. Detailed combustion models are validated using the simpler flow environment afforded by tests in microgravity. Once validated, they can be used to build more complex combustion models needed to capture the important details of flames burning in normal gravity. These models have wide applicability to the general understanding of many terrestrial combustion problems and will guide novel spacecraft design and ensure the safety of future crewed missions.

investigations.objective:
The primary goal of the FLEX-2 flight experiments is to extend the results of FLEX-1 to fuels and environmental conditions that mimic real combustor conditions, as well as, provide benchmark experimental data on bi-component droplet combustion over a wide range of initial conditions in order to validate numerical simulations and to develop new theoretical models.

Detailed experimental objectives can be further itemized as:
  1. Investigate the role of liquid-phase mixing on the burning characteristics of bi-component fuel droplets.
  2. Examine the steady and unsteady liquid and gas-phase phenomena in pure fuel combustion.
  3. Study flame extinction mechanisms and their boundaries.
  4. Analyze the soot formation process, including soot volume fraction soot-shell dynamics.
  5. Determine the influence of droplet interactions on the flammability limits and extinction behavior of droplet arrays.
  6. Validate theoretical models of droplet combustion through comprehensive experimental data collection in microgravity environments.
investigations.hypothesis: Fairly sophisticated numerical simulations of convective droplet combustion have been developed in the last decade where the key contribution is the inclusion of full Navier-Stokes equations for the gas-phase flow field. However, due to the inherent complexity of the problem, varying degrees of approximations have been made in treating the chemistry, radiation, and the coupling between the gas and liquid phases. The validity of the assumptions or the hypothesis used in these simulation have not been confirmed by using benchmark data. By conducting these experiments in a microgravity environment, the effects of buoyancy are minimized, and the droplet can be characterized only as a function of thermocapillary or solutalcapillary stresses allowing for a clear observation of the fundamental combustion processes,  The present FLEX-2 experiments using bi-component mixtures. In addition, the microgravity environment allows study of such phenomena as the transitions between radiative and diffusive extension of the flame. The primary goal of the flight experiments is to provide benchmark experimental data on bi-component droplet combustion over a wide range of initial conditions that could be used to validate numerical simulations and to develop new theoretical models.
investigations.approach:
The chamber was filled with the appropriate atmosphere, which was varied in pressure between 0.5 atm to 3.0 atm and O2 concentration between 0.1 to 0.4 mole fraction with the diluent gas making up the balance. A settling time of approximately 2 minutes  elapsed prior to initiating the test in order to ensure that the temperature and pressure of the chamber gases have stabilized. This settling time was followed by the dispensing of a predetermined amount of fuel (based on the target droplet size) onto the support fiber for those tests in which the droplet is not freely deployed. When sufficient fuel has been dispensed the dispensing needles were retracted and a dwell period of at least 10 seconds was allowed for the droplet internal fluid motion induced by deployment to subside. This was then followed by initiating power to the ignitor for a selectable amount of time ranging from 1 second to 5 seconds after which the ignitor was retracted from the field of view. If the flow field is to be generated by translating the droplet then droplet motion would commence at the same time that the ignitor is retracted. A near real-time download of the color camera video was employed in order to verify successful droplet deployment, ignition, and overall progress of the experiment. Pressure and temperature data of the chamber environment was also recorded in near real time.

The overall investigation approach can be summarized as:
  1. Test parameters are determined, including pressure, temperature, fuel mixture, and humidity.
  2. Fill the combustion chamber with the selected gas mixtures.
  3. Deploy the droplet(s) carefully controlling the droplet diameter.
  4. Allow the droplet to stabilize in the microgravity environment.
  5. Ignite the droplet in a uniform and controlled fashion.
  6. Monitor combustions and track flame evolution using high speed photography.
  7. Monitor and adjust experimental conditions as needed.
  8. Analyze data.

The independently varied experimental parameters during FLEX-2 experiments were 1) Fuel type 2) Ambient gas composition 3) Ambient Pressure 4) Droplet initial diameter 5) Droplet translation velocity (and acceleration) 6) Droplet spacing and initial size in a binary linear array.
investigations.research_impacts:
The combustion of liquid fuels is the overwhelming energy source in the transportation sector. Insights gained from these studies can lead to more efficient and cleaner combustion technologies which are crucial for reducing pollution and greenhouse gas emissions. By improving fuel efficiency and developing better fuels, these experiments can contribute to:

  1) More sustainable energy production.
  2) Future combustor designs with minimal carbon footprint, maximum fuel efficiency and less pollutant emissions.
  3) Allow quantitative evaluation of the performance of future fuels in combustors through the development of surrogates (mixtures of pure fuels that simulate the behavior of real fuels).
  4) Validation of jet engine models by engine manufacturers with support from prior droplet results.

investigations.objective: The FLEX (Flame Extinguishment Experiment) investigation aims to map the flammability limits of liquid fuels in microgravity environments, measure the effectiveness of various gaseous fire suppressants such as CO2, He, and SF6, and develop reliable predictive models for combustion limits under reduced gravity conditions. The mission seeks to validate and improve simplified models by incorporating detailed chemical reactions, heat transfer, and material movement, using both space-based data and extensive ground-based tests. Key flight experiment goals include obtaining high-resolution measurements of droplet burning rates, flame extinction behavior, heat radiation, soot levels, and temperature profiles, while systematically analyzing the effects of different ambient conditions and suppressant concentrations. These investigations are essential for advancing the fundamental understanding of combustion processes in microgravity and enhancing fire safety protocols for future space missions.
investigations.hypothesis: The primary hypothesis of the FLEX mission is that microgravity conditions fundamentally alter the combustion and extinction characteristics of liquid fuel droplets due to changes in species and energy transport dynamics, radiative heat loss, and chemical kinetics. Specifically, the hypothesis posits that the lack of buoyant convection in microgravity will lead to significant differences in the flammability limits and suppression efficacy of various fire suppressant agents compared to normal gravity conditions. This hypothesis underpins the design of the FLEX experiments, which aim to map flammability boundaries, quantify suppressant efficacy, and develop predictive models to improve fire safety in space environments.
investigations.approach:
The FLEX experiments involve igniting and observing the burning behavior of relatively large droplets. A primary objective of the experiments is to determine the Limiting Oxygen Index (LOI) as a function of ambient pressure and determine how the presence of a suppressant influences the LOI .
The basic outline of the procedure to construct this diagram is as follows:
  1. Select the test pressure (0.5 − 1.5 atm) for the LOI tests.
  2. Select a smaller droplet size (≈ 3 mm)
  3. Select an ambient oxygen mole fraction that, based on ground-based testing, will support droplets burning to completion (as opposed to extinguishing at a finite droplet size).
  4. Perform a droplet combustion test.
  5. Increase the droplet size or repeat the test (if finite extinction diameter at flame extinction observed).
  6. Continue steps 4 and 5 until flame exists for only a short time after ignition (radiative extinction).
  7. Continue steps 4 thru 6 at a decreased ambient oxygen mole fraction.
  8. Continue step 7 to an ambient oxygen mole fraction where the droplet does not ignite.

There were ambient conditions where the extinction droplet sizes at all ambient oxygen mole fractions were too small to either be observed or measured with the available diagnostics. In this case, the determination of the LOI is similar, but more iterative. Instead of observing flame extinction, however, the procedure  involved an iterative sequence of tests (burn to completion followed by a no ignition test) with progressively smaller increments in ambient oxygen mole fraction to determine the LOI . For the slow flow tests (in the flight experiment), the configuration of the flight hardware did not allow for adequate diagnostics over the entire test for a droplet in a uniform, steady convective flow.  In these tests, the procedure will be to duplicate tests above which yield finite-sized extinction droplet diameters. Near the end of the tests, prior to flame extinction, the droplet will be subjected to a small, sub-buoyant, convective flow (imparted by translating the droplet at a slow, uniform speed).

The goal of the experiment is then to see how the presence of this flow influences the extinction process. Note, a large number of the tests involve free droplets (as opposed to fiber-supported droplets) and a number of these tests will have droplets with a slow drift velocity. Data gathered from these tests to examine the influences of a small, sub-buoyant flow on both the burning and extinction process.
investigations.research_impacts: The research impacts and Earth benefits of the FLEX mission are significant and multifaceted. By enhancing our understanding of microgravity combustion, the mission directly contributes to improved fire safety protocols for future space missions, ensuring the safety of crew members in environments where traditional fire suppression methods may be ineffective. On Earth, the insights gained from these experiments have the potential to advance fire safety in confined and reduced-gravity environments, such as submarines or high-altitude aircraft. The mission's findings on the effectiveness of various fire suppressants, including CO2, He, and SF6, in microgravity can lead to the development of more efficient and less harmful fire suppression systems, reducing the risk of toxic byproducts during fire events. Additionally, the study of ''cool flames'' and low-temperature combustion processes observed in microgravity can inform the design of advanced combustion engines, leading to improved fuel efficiency and reduced emissions in automotive and industrial applications. Overall, the FLEX mission's contributions to combustion science have the potential to enhance both space exploration safety and terrestrial fire safety technologies.

investigations.title: Spacecraft Fire Experiment-III
moon_base_score_notes: crew-relevant solid materials
investigations.objective:
The objectives of this investigation were to:
(1) determine how rapidly a large scale fire grows in low-gravity and (2) investigate the low-g flammability limits compared to those obtained in NASA’s normal gravity material flammability screening test.
investigations.hypothesis: This investigation hypothesizes that due to large differences between fire behavior in normal and reduced gravity, the use of terrestrial fires and fire standards to design spacecraft fire safety systems presents an inherent risk to the vehicle because of the significant level of uncertainty. While this approach has been successful thus far, the uncertainty and risk will increase as exploration missions venture further from earth with considerably longer transit times for a safe return. There is a significant lack of microgravity data available for spacecraft designers on which to base their fire safety designs and procedures. To address this knowledge gap, this investigation proposed to conduct large-scale fire safety experiments in an expendable spacecraft without risk to a crew.
investigations.approach: The Saffire-III experiments were performed on the Orbital Science’s Cygnus resupply vehicle after it deberthed from the ISS. As a follow on to the Saffire 1 investigation, the Saffire III investigation also used SIBAL as the sample material. However, the experiments were conducted at a flow velocity of 30 cm/s compared to 20 cm/s during Saffire I. The flow was either concurrent or opposed.  Once the sample was ignited flame images were captured using two cameras. In addition, thermocouples provided flow, flame, and plume temperatures, two radiometers recorded flame radiation, solid state sensors were used to measure pressure, CO2 and O2 mole faction, and two anemometer tracked flow velocity. All data was compressed, and subsequently downlinked. Details related to samples and experimental parameters are provided in the Experimental Details file in the Science document folder.
investigations.research_impacts: The Saffire-I experiment provides a new way to study a realistic fire on an exploration vehicle, which has not been possible in the past because the risks are too high. Instruments on an unmanned cargo vessel measure oxygen, carbon dioxide, heat, pressure and flame growth, and two video cameras provide views of the flame. Results determine microgravity flammability limits for several spacecraft materials, help to validate NASA’s material selection criteria, and how microgravity and limited oxygen affect flame size. The investigation is crucial for the safety of current and future space missions. Studying fire in small, sealed environments such as the Cygnus cargo supply vehicle benefits fire safety and prevention efforts on Earth, including inside mines, airplanes, or submarines.

investigations.objective:
The focus of DAFT / DAFT-2 was to mitigate the risk for the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME). SAME relied on a commercially available condensate nuclei counter, the TSI P-Trak,  to quantify smoke aerosols in a microgravity environment, however there were concerns that th P-Trak would not be reliable in microgravity as it relies on gravity to recycle isopropyl alcohol used in the measurement process.
DAFT / DAFT-2 tests that a modified P-Trak particulate counter would be accurate in microgravity.

Summarized objectives include:
    1) Demonstrate the Functionality of the Modified TSI P-Trak in Microgravity
    2) Compare the TSI P-Trak Performance against the DustTrak control
    3) Create and Analyze Aerosol Standards in Microgravity
    4) Ensure the reliability of future aerosol experiments
investigations.hypothesis:
The TSI P-Trak operates by condensing isopropanol around aerosol particulates that are subsequently laser counted. It was hypothesized that the P-Trak would not work in microgravity due to two potential failure modes that exist. 1) the system would clog or become obscured by isopropanol, and 2) the internal air-flow dynamics of the optics chamber of the device will cause an over counting of particulates.

The TSI P-Trak was modified for microgravity use via using capillary action to recycle the isopropanol. Therefore, there are two basic hypotheses:
    1) that the P-Trak, as modified for use in SAME, would function normally in microgravity.
    2) that the aerosol created and filtered per the experiment design would be within the measurement capabilities of the test devices.
investigations.approach:
The experimental approach consists of the following components:

    1) Modification of Instrumentation: TSI P-Trak was modified for use in microgravity by redesigning the condenser tube to use capillary forces for recycling isopropyl alcohol and removing the mercury switch responsible for detecting instrument orientation.
    2) Aerosol Generation: Arizona Red Dust (ARD) was chosen as an aerosol standard due to its ease of dispersion. The ARD was aerosolized with GN2 to create particle samples. The aerosol was contained within 15-liter Mylar bags.
    3) On-Orbit Testing: The modified P-Trak gathered data from counting aerosol particles and these data were compared to the DustTrak CNC specifically designed to work in microgravity.
investigations.research_impacts: Extended duration space flight missions with larger vessels will require fire detection systems with increased reliability and sensitivity. This research will impact the development of novel fire and smoke detection systems for the International Space Station and future spacecrafts. Additionally, the successful adaptation of the TSI P-Trak for microgravity can inform the design of instruments for use in other challenging Earth environments, such as submarines or underwater laboratories where accurate detection of smoke can save lives.

    1) Examine the combustion behavior of n-dodecane and mixtures of n-dodecane/iso-dodecane at pressures ranging from 0.25 atm to 5 atm.
    2) Analyze the effects of helium dilution on cool flame behavior.
    3) Examine the behavior of combustion characteristics.
    4) Investigate the relationship between droplet size, pressure, and flame extinction, and (5) understand the consequence of soot formation during cool flame combustion.
investigations.hypothesis: Flame combustion of liquid hydrocarbon fuels such as n-dodecane, n-dodecane/iso-dodecane mixtures, and faresane in microgravity can provide insights into low-temperature chemical kinetics, revealing critical parameters like droplet extinction diameters and flame dynamics that are not observable on Earth.
investigations.approach: The Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) contains the Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus (MDCA) which facilitates the controlled combustion of fuel droplets. A system of gas bottles and fuel syringes delivers the desired gas mixture to the combustion chamber ranging from 0.25 to 0.5 atm. Droplets of fuel are dispensed and suspended between hypodermic needles or tethered using silicon-carbide fibers. A hot-wire igniter is positioned near the droplet for ignition. After ignition the wire is retracted. Fuels observed include n-dodecane, farnesane, and mixtures of n-dodecane/iso-dodecane. Fuels diluted with molecular oxygen, atomic nitrogen, and helium to study the influence on flame extinction and dynamics. Flames were observed with a black-and-white camera for droplet size measurements. A UV camera was used for capturing the OH* radical emissions and flame size. Other high resolution cameras were used for monitoring and documentation. Narrow-band and wide-band radiometers for analyzed flame radiation.
investigations.research_impacts:
A basic understanding of cool flames is important for understanding ignition phenomena of practical fuels and fuel additives. Cool flames play a key role in the development and selection of new fuels and the design of advanced engines such as clean, high-efficiency Homogeneous Charge Compression Ignition (HCCI) engines. The research will also help combustion chemists to develop new computational models to compute combustion performance in for many practical applications on earth, including an understanding of how cool flame reactivity determines octane and cetane number for fuels in spark ignition and diesel engines.
Cool Flames Investigation (CFI) will provide critical validation for complex chemical kinetic mechanisms, advance the understanding of flame dynamics and instabilities in low-temperature combustion, and support the design of safer spacecraft systems by refining knowledge of combustion in microgravity environments.

a. Objectives

Cool flame phenomena are influenced by a number of factors, including the fuel molecular structure (for 
pure fuel cases), the ambient environment (pressure, temperature, oxygen and diluent (He) concentrations), 
and the fuel composition (the mixture of fuel structures and perhaps fuel additives such as those used to 
change octane or cetane behavior). Though it is not possible to examine all of these factors in a thorough 
manner, here we propose a set of experiments that explore each one of these factors, namely, fuel structure 
effects, ambient conditions effect, fuel mixture effects, and the presence of fuel additives.

investigations.objective:
1. Plan and support flight testing on the International Space Station (ISS).
2. Determine the conditions for which cool diffusion flames occur for propane, n-butane, and n-pentane; normal and inverse flames; and a broad range of Zst, Tad, and fluent flow rate.
3. Support the flight tests with advanced CFD simulations.
4. Identify or develop a chemical kinetics mechanism that yields good agreement between the CFD predictions and the ISS measurements.
5. Disseminate the results as widely as possible.
investigations.hypothesis:
The hypotheses of this research are that testing aboard the ISS can demonstrate the following for the first time, contributing to an improved understanding of cool flame kinetics.
  1. Steady-state cool diffusion flames on spherical porous burners.
  2. Cool diffusion flames burning propane, n-butane, and n-pentane.
  3. Cool diffusion flames for a wide range of Zst, Tad, and pressures.
  4. Inverse cool diffusion flames.
  5. Cool diffusion flames for which a decrease in fluent flow rate will cause extinction, whereas an increase will cause a transition to a hot diffusion flame, with oscillation possible between hot and cool flames.
investigations.approach: Perform spherical diffusion flame tests aboard the International Space Station. Consider multiple fuels, a range of reactant dilutions, flow rates, and pressures for normal and inverse convection directions. Observe the flames with a broad suite of cameras, radiometers, photomultiplier tubes, and thermocouples.
investigations.research_impacts: Combustion provides 86% of the world’s energy and an even higher fraction of the energy used for transportation. The internal combustion engines used for transportation generally have thermal efficiencies of 38% or lower because of thermal losses. These efficiencies may increase to 60% if future engines can take advantage of ultra-lean combustion. However, this progress is being impeded by the limited understanding of the chemistry of cool flames. Research into cool diffusion flames (whose peak temperatures are 500 – 1000 K) has grown exponentially since they were discovered in 2012.  The measurements performed for this project will help to test and advance cool flame kinetics mechanisms. This should facilitate the development of more efficient internal combustion engines.

investigations.title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames
investigations.objective: The objective of this investigation is to better understand the relationship between electric field voltage and chemi-ion current, analyze the dynamic response of flames to electric field changes, evaluate soot formation, and characterize stabilized near-limit lifted flames.
investigations.hypothesis: The application of electric fields in microgravity environments will significantly influence laminar diffusion flames by enabling precise manipulation of flame stability, soot behavior, and combustion dynamics through ion-driven convection and chemi-ionization processes.
investigations.approach:
The E-FIELD flames experiment investigates how electric fields influence the behavior of laminar diffusion flames in microgravity. This unique environment is ideal for isolating electric field effects from buoyancy forces.
The experiment is conducted with gas-fueled flames, both with and without a coflow of air. In the former case, the tests are conducted using the same coflow burner used by the Coflow Laminar Diffusion (CLD) Flame experiment. An electric field is generated by creating a high voltage (up to 10 kV) differential between the burner and a flat circular mesh suspended above (i.e., downstream of) the burner. Measurements, as a function of the field strength and fuel, are taken of the ion current through the flame and the flame’s response time to electric forcing. The gas-jet burner is used to create a small, focused flame for detailed ion-driven convection studies while the coflow burner surrounds the fuel jet with a weak synthetic air flow to enable flame stability and soot behavior analysis. A high-voltage copper mesh electrode positioned above the burner tip generated an electric field with controlled polarity and strength. The electric field interacts with ions generated through chemi-ionization during combustion, driving ion-driving convection and influencing flame behavior. Methane and ethylene were used as fuels and diluted with nitrogen to control flame strength. Dilution levels were varied to explore a range of combustion dynamics, from highly stable to near-extinction flames. Voltage-current curves were recorded to assess the relationship between electric field strength and chemi-ion current, revealing ion-driven convection effects. High-resolution cameras captured flame shape, luminosity, and soot distribution. Spectral imaging with filters measures chemiluminescent emissions and soot volume fraction. There were thermopile detectors to measure flame radiant emissions.
All experiments were conducted in the combustion integrated rack (CIR). Tests were administered with Glenn Research Center (GRC) directing astronaut actions. Parameters such as fuel flow rate, coflow velocity, and field polarity are were varied to isolate specific effects on ion production, flame stability, and soot behavior.
investigations.research_impacts: The E-FIELD Flames research is not being conducted to serve any space applications, but it is possible that its findings could aid the development of future space-based combustion devices (e.g., for solid waste processing). The use of electric fields to control flames can reduce the production of harmful pollutants in practical terrestrial combustion. The combustion of fossil fuel is the primary human source of greenhouse gas and acid rain and furthermore creates soot, which can be beneficial but is also a health hazard. Combustion using electrical fields may also allow for more efficient combustion, reducing fuel consumption in addition to unwanted emissions.

Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME)

PURPOSE:  ACME is focused on advanced combustion 
technology via fundamental microgravity research.  The 
primary goal is to improve efficiency and reduce pollutant 
emission in practical terrestrial combustion.  A secondary 
objective is fire prevention, especially for spacecraft. 
 
RESEARCH:  ACME includes six independent experiments 
investigating laminar, gaseous, non-premixed flames.  They 
are being conducted with a single set of modular hardware 
in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International 
Space Station (ISS).

STATUS:  ACME set-up and check-out was carried out by the 
ISS crew in Sept.-Oct. 2017, where science testing began in 
November.  The first round of testing for the Coflow Laminar 
Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) experiment of Marshall B. Long 
et al. was completed in Feb. 2018, where 130 methane 
flames (at a range of concentrations) were ignited.  The first 
round of testing for the Electric-Field Effects on Laminar 
Diffusion Flames (E-FIELD Flames) experiment of Derek 
Dunn-Rankin et al. was completed on May 18, where 120 
coflow flames were ignited.  On May 20, burners and 
additional hardware for the next three ACME experiments 
are scheduled to launch.  The ACME hardware should be 
reconfigured on May 22 by astronaut Ricky Arnold (NASA) 
for CLD Flame’s second round, where the ethylene flame 
testing should begin later in the week.

electric field can be used to manipulate the ions and control non-premixed flames for practical

with reduced pollutant emission, i.e., where the flame is not reliably sustained without the 
electric field.  As another example, the role of electric fields on soot formation can be dramatic.

residence time of the soot precursors within the hot flame.  The experiment contributes to our

A. Determine the relationship between electric field voltage and chemi-ion current as

functions of total fuel (methane and ethylene) flow rate and the amount of inert

B. Obtain the time response of the flame chemiluminescence, luminosity, and the ion

current to large step changes in voltage, as functions of total fuel (methane and ethylene) 
flow rate and amount of inert (nitrogen) added to the fuel stream. 
C. Evaluate and manipulate sooting behavior (i.e., soot volume fraction and location of

luminous soot) in relation to the electric field voltage and chemi-ion current as functions 
of total fuel (methane and ethylene) flow rate and amount of inert (nitrogen) added to 
the fuel stream. 
D. Use the variation of the chemi-ion current as a function of applied voltage to characterize

the combustion behavior of near-limit lifted flames and use the associated ion-driven 
wind to stabilize or reattach these flames.

flame and electric field conditions.  The fuel, fuel jet velocity, air flow, electric-field voltage and

electrode configuration (close to a plane-to-plane) than the jet burner (close to a point-to-plane).

Burning Rate Emulator (BRE)
• Objective: Fire Safety—To improve our fundamental understanding of materials ﬂammability, such 
   as extinction behavior and the conditions needed for sustained combustion, and to assess the 
   relevance of existing ﬂammability test methods for low- and partial-gravity environments.
• Flame/Burner: Flat perforated disk fed with gaseous fuel to simulate the burning of solid and 
   liquid fuels, where measurements are made of the thermal feedback upon which the vaporization 
   of such fuels depend.
• Investigators: Profs. James G. Quintiere and Peter B. Sunderland, University of Maryland; and 
   Dr. John L. deRis, FM Global (retired)

• Objective: Energy and Environment—To extend the range of ﬂame conditions that can be 
   accurately predicted by computational models, especially for highly dilute and heavily 
   sooting conditions.
• Flame/Burner: Coﬂow ﬂame where the gaseous fuel issues from an inner tube, which is centered 
   within a much larger outer tube, where an oxygen/nitrogen mixture issues from the annulus. 
• Investigators: Profs. Marshall B. Long and Mitchell D. Smooke, Yale University

Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames (E-FIELD Flames)
• Objective: Energy and Environment—To gain an improved understanding of ion production in ﬂames 
   and investigate how an electric ﬁeld can be used to control ﬂames through the ion-driven wind.
• Flame/Burner: Gas-jet ﬂame, where (1) the gaseous fuel issues from a small circular tube into a 
   still atmosphere and (2) a high-voltage electric ﬁeld is established between the burner and a 
   disk-shaped copper mesh located a few centimeters downstream of the burner. 
• Investigator: Prof. Derek Dunn-Rankin, University of California, Irvine

Coﬂow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame)

• Objective: Energy and Environment—To improve our understanding of soot inception and control in 
   order to enable (1) the “design” of nonpremixed ﬂames that are both robust and soot free and (2) the 
   optimization of oxygen-enriched combustion.
• Flame/Burner: Spherical ﬂame where the burner gas issues from a porous spherical burner. Tests 
   are planned for both (1) normal ﬂames, where the fuel ﬂows into an oxygen/inert atmosphere and 
   (2) inverse ﬂames, where an oxygen/inert mixture ﬂows into a fuel atmosphere.
• Investigators: Prof. Richard L. Axelbaum, Washington University in St. Louis; Prof. Beei-Huan Chao, 
   University of Hawaii; Prof. Peter B. Sunderland, University of Maryland; and Dr. David L. Urban, 
   NASA Glenn Research Center

What Is Microgravity?
	
Gravity is a force that governs motion 
throughout the universe. It holds us to the 
ground and keeps the Earth in orbit around the 
Sun. Microgravity describes the environment 
in orbital space flight, which has very weak 
gravitational effects (one-millionth of what is 
felt on Earth) and which is sometimes referred 
to as a state of “weightlessness.” The condition 
of microgravity occurs when an object is in 
“free fall.” In free fall, an object falls faster and 
faster, accelerating with exactly the speed of 
attraction caused by gravity. Objects travelling 
around the Earth in a state of continuous free 
fall, or orbit, are essentially weightless even 
though their mass remains the same.

Conducting research in a microgravity 
environment gives researchers a unique oppor­
tunity to study the true nature of processes and 
materials without having to consider the effects 
of Earth’s gravity. Thus, physics theories can be 
tested at levels of accuracy that are impossible 
on Earth. Microgravity experiments uncover the 
mystery of how gravity affects processes such 
as combustion science and fluid physics. This 
knowledge can then help to improve the way 
we do things on Earth.

investigations.title: Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment
investigations.objective:
The objective of SPICE is to better understand the complex process of combustion by observing flames in a microgravity environment aboard the International Space Station (ISS) and analogous ground experiments.

Specific objectives were:
(1) Identify the laminar smoke-point properties of non-buoyant jet diffusion flames under various co-flow conditions in microgravity.
(2) Determine the effects of burner diameter and co-flow velocity on the luminous flame lengths and smoke points.
(3) Quantify the sooting propensity of different fuels, such as ethylene, propane, and propylene mixtures.
(4) Validate the correlation between luminous flame shape and residence time under microgravity conditions.
(5) Investigate the impact of air and fuel flow rate variations on smoke point phenomena in space.
investigations.hypothesis: The research hypothesizes that by minimizing gravity-driven transport phenomena scientists can study the laminar smoke-point properties of non-buoyant jet diffusion flames. Flame properties are expected to differ significantly from those observed under normal gravity.
investigations.approach: The experimental setup in the microgravity science glovebox consisted of an apparatus with a flow duct with integrated nozzles, cameras, and fuel delivery systems. Fuels tested included methane, ethylene, propane, propylene, and propylene mixtures. Each flame was ignited in a controlled co-flow air environment, with burner diameters of 0.41 mm, 0.76 mm, and 1.6 mm and co-flow velocities ranging from 5.4 cm/s to 65 cm/s. Fuel flow rates were adjusted to identify the smoke point, marked by the flame's transition to emitting soot. Data such as flame lengths were recorded using still and video cameras. Measurements included flame height, radiative heat losses, and co-flow air velocity distributions. In total 526 flames were studied.
investigations.research_impacts:
(1) Will improve our understanding of soot formation mechanisms and help design safer spacecraft environments.
(2) Will contribute to refining our computational models for predicting flame behaviors under non-buoyant conditions.
(3) Will enhance our knowledge of soot generation
(4) Could possibly provide insights to better fuel formulations and combustion processes.

SMOKE POINTS OF MICROGRAVITY AND 
NORMAL GRAVITY COFLOW DIFFUSION 
FLAMES   
 
 
 
Keenan Thomas Dotson, M.S., 2009 
 
 
Directed By: 
Assistant Professor, Peter B. Sunderland, 
Department of Fire Protection Engineering 
 
 
Smoke points were measured in microgravity aboard the International Space Station

(ISS) as part of the Smoke Points in Coflow Experiment (SPICE), and in normal

gravity conditions. In microgravity conditions increasing the coflow velocity or

decreasing the burner diameter increased the smoke point flame length. A simplified

prediction of centerline jet velocity did not yield residence-time-based criticalities or

data collapse. Simulation of non-reacting flows showed that the simplified centerline

velocity prediction was able to predict velocity decay for only relatively weak

coflows. An improved model may yield different results. In normal earth gravity

coflow velocity exhibited mixed effects. For burner diameters of 0.41, 0.76, and 1.6

mm, smoke points increased with increases of coflow velocity. For an unconfined

coflow burner with a burner diameter of 13.7 mm smoke point length decreased with

increasing coflow velocity for ethylene and propylene, while increasing for propane

flames.

Hypothesis 
The hypothesis of the SPICE investigation is that smoke point behavior

will be observed for co-flowing flames and that it will show 
dependence on nozzle diameter and coflow velocity. 
 
B. 
Objectives of Investigation 
The objective of the SPICE experiment is to find the laminar smoke-point 
properties of nonbuoyant jet diffusion flames (i.e., the properties of the 
largest laminar jet diffusion flames that do not emit soot) for several fuels 
under different nozzle diameter/ co-flow velocity configurations.  
Luminous flame shape measurements would also be made to verify 
models of the flame shapes under co-flow conditions.  
 
C. 
Previous Mission Experience 
 
N/A 
 
D. 
Background/History of Project (Optional) 
 
The SPICE experiment was an outgrowth of the Laminar Soot Processes 
Experiment (LSP) which flew on STS 83, 94, and 107.  SPICE utilized the 
design heritage and modified the hardware from the Enclosed Laminar Flames 
Experiment (ELF) which flew in the Middeck Glovebox on STS 87. 
 
II.  Methods/Research Operations

A. 
Discussion of Method/Protocol 
 
Most tests were conducted by setting the coflow velocity, igniting the flame, 
and adjusting the fuel flow rate. Approximate smoke points were identified in 
the video by the flight crew and simultaneously by the ground support crew in 
Cleveland. Typical burn times were 60 s, and after each two such burns the 
MSG contents were flushed with ISS cabin air.  After the tests the video 
record was analyzed to identify smoke point conditions. The associated 
coflow and fuel flow rates were obtained from digital data recorded in the 
video. The smoke point lengths, LSP, were obtained from the video record 
and are the measured distance from the burner tip to the tip of the luminous 
flame on the flame axis.

III. Results

A. 
List of Preflight, In-flight, Postflight Anomalies 
 
SPICE operated very successfully with the only significant anomaly being the 
accumulation of soot in the outlet screen which changed the flow behavior in 
the duct.  This was corrected by a crew member using the vacuum to clean the 
outlet screen on June 15. 
B. 
Completeness/Quality of Data 
During Increment 18 SPICE conducted 108 test points completing its nominal 
test matrix. During Increments 19/20 SPICE conducted 155 additional test 
points the provided improved resolution of the smoke points and allowed us to 
explore further limits in the parameter space.

investigations.title: Structure and Liftoff In Combustion Experiment
investigations.objective:
Objective: The objective of this investigation is to better understand the structure and stability of laminar diffusion flames in microgravity.

Specific objectives of this investigation were:
1. To investigate the structure of laminar diffusion flames in microgravity to understand the stabilizing mechanisms at the flames base.
2. Determine the liftoff velocity limits for different fuels and burner diameters.
3. Evaluate the impact of fuel dilution with nitrogen on soot formation and flame stability.
4. Quantify the effects of microgravity on flame length and radiative heat loss compared to normal gravity conditions.
5. Validate numerical models for flame dynamics, soot production, and thermal radiation in non-premixed flames.
investigations.hypothesis: The hypothesis is that the structure and stability of laminar diffusion flames in microgravity are significantly influenced by burner diameter, coflow velocity, and fuel composition and are fundamentally different than flames observed on Earth.
investigations.approach: The SLICE apparatus consisted of a fan-driven flow duct, exchangeable burner tubes, and integrated sensors to measure flow rates and temperature. This setup used several fuels such as methane, ethylene, and nitrogen-diluted mixtures. Flames were then manually ignited and observed under controlled coflow air conditions. A high resolution camera captured still images while sensor data was overlaid on these images. Calibration tests for airflow velocity, soot measurement, and the fans were conducted to ensure the accuracy of the results. More than 4,000 high-resolution images were captured across 13 testing experiments. Data was then analyzed to correlate flame structure with stability with flow dynamics and fuel properties.
investigations.research_impacts:
1. Improved numerical models for flame behavior lead to more efficient combustion technologies on Earth.
2. Understanding soot formation aids in designing combustion systems with minimum emissions.
3. Insights into flame stability and behavior to enhance fire safety.
4. Findings will inform the development of cleaner, more efficient engines and industrial burners.
